title: Why things keep moving
scope: Choose the objectives in your school’s topic list. These are original practice questions with illustrative values, not a claim of an official school paper format.

objectives.label: Explain and use interactions.
objectives.note: A force describes an interaction between objects, such as contact or gravity.

objectives.label: Explain and use after release.
objectives.note: Once contact ends, the pushing hand no longer exerts a contact force on the released object.

objectives.label: Explain and use idealisation.
objectives.note: An idealised situation leaves out selected influences to reveal a simpler relationship.

objectives.label: Explain and use newton’s first law.
objectives.note: Zero resultant force means constant velocity, including the special case of remaining at rest.

objectives.label: Explain and use friction.
objectives.note: A contact force opposing relative sliding or its tendency at a surface.

cards.definition: A force describes an interaction between objects, such as contact or gravity.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A student sees a rolling ball stop and concludes that motion always needs a forward force. Explain what her evidence overlooks. The surface and air exert resistive forces. The stopping observation does not describe motion with zero resultant force.
cards.confusion: A moving object does not need a continuing forward force merely to keep moving.
cards.question: Explain interactions from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: A force describes an interaction between objects, such as contact or gravity. A moving object does not need a continuing forward force merely to keep moving.

cards.definition: Once contact ends, the pushing hand no longer exerts a contact force on the released object.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A coin has left a person’s fingers and is moving upwards. Ignoring air resistance, name the force acting on it and its direction, and explain whether the fingers still exert a force. Gravity acts downwards. There is no remaining upward contact force from the fingers after release.
cards.confusion: A push is not a substance stored inside the object.
cards.question: Explain after release from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Once contact ends, the pushing hand no longer exerts a contact force on the released object. A push is not a substance stored inside the object.

cards.definition: An idealised situation leaves out selected influences to reveal a simpler relationship.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: An ideal simulation shows a puck moving forever. A real puck stops. Explain one consistent reason. The ideal simulation neglects resistance. The real puck experiences resistive forces that change its velocity.
cards.confusion: Removing friction in a model is different from claiming no real surface has friction.
cards.question: Explain idealisation from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: An idealised situation leaves out selected influences to reveal a simpler relationship. Removing friction in a model is different from claiming no real surface has friction.

cards.definition: Zero resultant force means constant velocity, including the special case of remaining at rest.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A car turns at constant speed. Explain why the first law does not imply zero resultant force. The direction of its velocity changes. A resultant force is needed to change that velocity.
cards.confusion: Constant speed along a curve is not constant velocity.
cards.question: Explain newton’s first law from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: Zero resultant force means constant velocity, including the special case of remaining at rest. Constant speed along a curve is not constant velocity.

cards.definition: A contact force opposing relative sliding or its tendency at a surface.
cards.explanation: Use the relationship in the stated conditions and name the objects or system being considered.
cards.example: A box slides right across a floor. State the direction of the floor’s friction on the box and explain. The friction acts left. It opposes the box’s sliding relative to the floor.
cards.confusion: Friction is not always opposite the object’s motion relative to the ground.
cards.question: Explain friction from memory. What common mistake must you avoid?
cards.answer: A contact force opposing relative sliding or its tendency at a surface. Friction is not always opposite the object’s motion relative to the ground.
